The post Meta FAIR Releases e-means: An Algorithm Beating k-means in 10x Fewer Epochs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta FAIR researchers have released e-means , a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means algorithm. The e-means clustering algorithm reaches the loss Lloyd’s k-means gets in 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs . It ships in FAISS 1.16.0 under faiss.contrib.e_means . For anyone building vector indexes, quantizers or data-curation pipelines, clustering is often the slowest offline step. e-means targets exactly that step. TL;DR Size: It is an algorithm. Tested from 100K to 10 billion points, up to 16.7M clusters. Runs on: CPU or GPU, with PyTorch tensors or NumPy. Paper GPU runs use H100s. Performance: Lower loss than Lloyd’s k-means in roughly one-tenth the epochs, across 24 dataset configurations (self-reported). Best: 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over Flash-KMeans at equal loss. Worst: 16M-centroid runs need 64 GiB of float32 accumulators, so centroids must be sharded across GPUs. What is e-means? e-means is a mini-batch k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that updates centroids with exponential moving averages. How does e-means work? Every k-means variant keeps a sum S and a count N per cluster. The centroid is S divided by N. Methods differ only in how S and N change. Lloyd recomputes S and N from the full dataset each iteration. MacQueen (1967) keeps adding batch statistics forever, so stale assignments never leave. e-means decays old statistics at rate α: S ← (1−α)S + αs, and the same for N. Older assignments fade, so centroids track recent data. The research team expa Lloyd is a corner case: full batch with α = 1. On DEEP, that corner sits 1.8% above the best loss. The team tested plain gradient descent as an alternative. At its best setting, it ended 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above EMA. The authors suspect EMA wins because centroids always stay inside the hull of their assigned points. What replaces hyperparameter tuning? Two fitted scaling laws set batch size B and initial step α0 from dataset size n, cluster count k and epochs T. On held-out datasets, median regret was 0.07% for the step law. The step then follows a cosine schedule from α0 to 0.1α0. What else changed? Dead-cluster revival: clusters below a size threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. Finalization: training ends on each cluster’s exact last-epoch mean. Fused GPU kernels: nearest-centroid assignment is fused, so saved epochs become saved seconds. [EMBED: e-means interactive explainer] How fast is e-means in benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by the authors. Epochs: e-means beats Lloyd’s 25-epoch loss in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs. GPU: 10-45x wall-clock speedup against Flash-KMeans . CPU: 8-15x speedup against Faiss k-means. VIBE benchmark: all 11 embedding datasets needed 1.6 to 2.4 epochs. Billion scale: DINO10B, 10 billion 1,024-dim embeddings, split into 16.7M clusters in 2.5 epochs. The release thread shows a 1-CPU-thread demo. Lloyd took 4.39 s for 25 epochs. e-means took 0.43 s for 2.2 epochs. One Lloyd step touched 100,000 points (0.176 s). One e-means step touched 512 points (0.001 s). Mini-batch noise also helps escape bad local minima. On a 5-blob toy, Lloyd stayed stuck on 46% of 200 starts. e-means stayed stuck on 0%. Revival matters at large k. On DEEP with 16,384 clusters, proportional splitting left 47 dead clusters (0.3%). With revival off, 4,313 clusters (26.3%) died. How does e-means compare with other k-means options? It clones voices, steers delivery word by word and runs in real time in the browser The post Zyphra Releases ZONOS3-Mini: Open-Source TTS With 100M Active Parameters appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Zyphra has released ZONOS3-Mini , an open-source text-to-speech model built for real-time use on local devices. The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. TL;DR Size: 800M total parameters, about 100M active per token (64 experts, top-2 routing); 32,768-position context; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation. Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang-Omni, Apple Silicon via MLX, CPU/CUDA/Metal/Vulkan via ggml, and phones or laptops via WebGPU in the browser. Performance: Ranks first among open models on Zyphra’s ZTTS2-Eval Capability Index (self-reported). Best: 80 ms median time to first audio on one H100 at 8 concurrent requests, and 457 seconds of audio per second peak throughput. Worst: Under 570 ms time to first audio in the browser on a Pixel 9, versus under 150 ms on an M3 MacBook Air. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level open TTS quality at 100M active parameters. Worst: every benchmark is run by Zyphra itself, and reference-clip cloning scores far lower than embedding mode. What is ZONOS3-Mini? ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. How does the ZONOS3-Mini architecture work?
